newsitem.title: JAPAN: Foreign spirits makers condemn Japan on liquor tax.
newsitem.headline: Foreign spirits makers condemn Japan on liquor tax.

text.p: Spirits producers from Europe, the United States and Canada condemned Japan Friday for its reluctance to end a system of taxing imported liquor more severely than similar domestic products.
Japan has been ordered by the World Trade Organisation to end the disparity in the tax rates.

"The two days of discussions with politicians and government officials (in Tokyo) have left us very frustrated and very disappointed," Tim Jackson, chairman of the Trade Committee of the European Confederation of Spirits Producers, told a news conference.
Last month, the World Trade Organisation, ruling on a complaint by the European Union, the United States and Canada, found that Japan taxes imported spirits unfairly compared with domestic liquor.

"Japan has lost. The best solution would be for Japan to make the necessary reform and implementation by instituting a uniform, single rate for all spirit drinks based on alcohol content at the first opportunity. In other words, the budget for next year," Jackson said.

He said that Japan taxes imported spirits such as brandy and whiskey at rates of four to seven times as those imposed on popular domestic products such as shochu, which is a potent, colourless liquor made from barley. Taxes for gin, rum and vodka are about two to three times higher than shochu, he said.
Jackson said that Japanese officials and politicians assured them Tokyo will eventually comply with the WTO ruling. But he said they were looking at a long transition period.

Japan told the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body on Wednesday that it would make its laws conform to the finding, but that it would need time to shape the necessary measures. Under WTO rules, Japan has about 15 months to comply.
Tokyo has argued that shochu is largely a working class drink on which the price could not be raised.

Japan carries out a review of its entire taxation system towards the end of the year and relevant legislation is submitted to parliament early the following year. This would take effect from the start of the fiscal year on April 1.

"Either it accepts the WTO ruling and acts accordingly, or in our view, it will stand condemned as merely paying lip service to the rules of international trade which Japan itself has already signed up to," Jackson said.
